query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a trace amount of a segregation‐promoting element (e.g., Nb) during alloy synthesis will strengthen the lamellar colony interfaces by promoting interfacial segregation, thereby delaying microcrack initiation and simultaneously improving both the tensile strength and the room‐temperature ductility of eutectic high-entropy alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies. Its internal boundaries are relatively weak, leading to microcrack initiation under room-temperature tensile deformation, yielding a high strength but low ductility baseline.
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor addition (approximately 1–3 wt%) of Nb during alloy processing to promote segregation of Nb atoms to the lamellar interfaces. Follow this with a heat-treatment that enhances segregation without forming brittle intermetallic compounds.
generation.conditions: Standard processing for eutectic high-entropy alloys with controlled heat treatment to allow Nb segregation; experiments conducted at room temperature under tensile loading.
generation.structural_mediator: Strengthened lamellar interfaces due to Nb segregation that reduces interface energy and promotes better atomic bonding at phase boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The Nb atoms preferentially segregate to the lamellar boundaries during post-solidification heat treatment. This segregation reinforces the interfaces, inhibiting early crack nucleation by improving cohesive strength along the colony boundaries. Simultaneously, the strengthened interfaces help maintain ductility by delaying the propagation of microcracks during deformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, the Nb-alloyed alloy will show an increase in both tensile strength and room-temperature ductility. Microstructural analysis will indicate clearer evidence of Nb enrichment at the interfaces, correlating with fewer microcrack initiation sites under tensile testing.
generation.baseline: Unmodified eutectic high-entropy alloy displaying high strength but limited ductility due to early microcrack formation at weak lamellar interfaces.
generation.boundary: The improvement is expected only if the Nb addition is kept low enough to avoid forming continuous brittle phases. The beneficial effect requires proper heat treatment to promote interfacial segregation. Excessive Nb or inappropriate thermal processing may instead lead to embrittlement.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal Nb concentration and heat-treatment parameters for achieving effective segregation without inducing brittle phase precipitation remain to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of eutectic high-entropy alloy samples with 0%, 1%, 2%, and 3% Nb additions. Apply identical heat-treatment schedules designed to foster elemental segregation. Perform room-temperature tensile tests to measure strength and ductility. Use electron microscopy and atom probe tomography to assess the degree and distribution of Nb segregation at the lamellar interfaces.
measurements: Interfacial segregation profiles (via atom probe or high-resolution TEM)
Volume fraction and morphology of potential Nb-rich precipitates
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, compared to the baseline, the Nb-alloyed samples do not exhibit a statistically significant enhancement in both tensile strength and ductility, or if evidence of excessive Nb-induced brittle phase formation is observed, the hypothesis would be falsified.
